utterances.text: Okay. Do you have any knowledge as to what the crime police would do in the event that they determined that the fire was set by military personnel?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me turn to another topic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one clarifying question. You just said: "Our reports were sent to the police stations in the field and also to the crime police at the level of the police administration and also at the level of the ministry, which then processed them in their criminal reports when they decided to make -- to file criminal reports." Now, a few minutes ago, you were asked about the data on all the fires that were not results of combat activities; therefore, had other causes were sent by fire-fighting units to the criminal police, you said. And then the question was: "Which criminal police would they send it to?" And you said: "To the criminal police at the seat of the ministry. I assume that they also forwarded this to the relevant police administration in the field, so in Knin or elsewhere, wherever the fire occurred." So a couple of minutes ago, it was just an assumption that they would sent it to the local police authorities; whereas, now, you state, if I understood you well, that they were sent to the police stations in the field. What made the difference between the assumption five minutes ago and, now, it not being an assumption anymore, but a statement what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the events that occurred in the field were obviously recorded in such a way that they would end up in a certain police station; that is, police administration, in the field. From there, the reports were also coming to the headquarters of the OP Povratak, and there we had uniformed police, crime police, and all other types of police. In certain regular analysis that were undertaken, it was obviously clear that the crime police would undertake certain additional investigation of any suspicious fires and proceed with criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not an answer to my question. The same problem you had with your last question, Mr. Misetic, that the answer given was not an answer to your question. May I ask you to well consider what the question is, and then to give an answer to the question, focussing on what the person who asks the question would like to know. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zidovec, turning your attention to reception centres. My first question to you is: To your knowledge, did you receive any -- let me rephrase it. Did you receive any reports that international organisations, whether the Red Cross, Amnesty International, the United Nations, et cetera, criticised Croatia's establishment of reception centres for civilians?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: No, I have never received any such reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the people that were housed in the reception centres during and after Operation Storm, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: In the reception centres, there were citizens of both Croatian and Serbian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Chamber why reception centres were established?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: The first order to set up reception centres was signed by me on August the 4th, under the assumption that, obviously immediately after the combat activities, the population of the area will need assistance. We requested the cooperation from the government office for refugees and also the cooperation of local institutions, primarily social welfare centres. However, the situation in the field was such that these centres were mostly set up by ourselves, in different school facilities and other similar public facilities which could receive the population. And then, again, we would ask for cooperation and assistance of the relevant institutions such as social welfare centres and other services.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Were the reception centres set up as part of a plan to remove Serb civilians from the liberated areas?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any information which indicated to you that within the reception centres fear was deliberately being instilled in Serb civilians so as to encourage them to leave Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: I have never been informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you have -- or did you receive any information that Serb civilians were systematically being transferred out of the reception centres to locations outside of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: We have not received any such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Would the authorities transfer people to these reception centres against their well, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Were people allowed to leave the reception centres once they had entered?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you explain what the procedure was if a person wished to leave the reception centre?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: Such a person was erased from some basic records that we kept, and the relevant social welfare centres would be informed about this; also, the respective Red Cross unit, but I'm not sure that this was a rule. What was certainly the case was that any such person was allowed to leave a reception centre at any time he or she wished to do that, in order to return home or to go anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What about persons who were determined to be incapable of living by themselves? Sick, elderly? How would those people ultimately leave a reception centre?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: For such persons, we requested the social welfare centres to take care about them and also Red Cross units, in order to provide the necessary logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Turning your attention to the issue of the -- to paragraph 23 of your statement, I should say, which is your statement that in the aftermath of Operation Storm, civilian protection units examined -- should say 48.000 houses, primarily for the purposes of sanitation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question in relation to the last series of questions about the reception centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, Mr. Zidovec, your answer about everyone being free to leave the reception centre, would that be equally true for men, including able-bodied men, women, children? Would it be true for everyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This rule obviously applied to everybody who was in a reception centre. The old people who were, indeed, in the reception centre were mostly elderly, some of them entirely incapacitated, unable to move, who were brought there by their relatives because there was nobody else in the surrounding area who would be able to take care about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But were there also able-bodied men, and were they sometimes questioned about their past? And would they also be free to leave the reception centres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In our reception centres that were set up by the civil protection, we had no such questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just following up on the Presiding Judge's questions, do you know what the difference was between a reception centre and a collection centre?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: The population that went to the reception centres was the population whose basic living was jeopardised. There they were provided with fundamental medical care, and they were -- the proposals were made to organise their social security and obviously certain hygienic functions were carried out. So certain elementary assistance was provided by the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. But do you know what a collection centre was?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: I assume on the basis of a document which was shown to me here, a document of the crime police, that they referred to centres where they could have arrested soldiers or members of some military formations, but civilian protection had nothing to do with such collection centres. Our centres were exclusively of a humanitarian nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, going back to paragraph 23 of your statement, why was the civil protection examining 48.000 houses?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: There were two main reasons. First, the apartments and houses were examined to establish if there were any bodies in there; and, secondly, also certain sanitation measures, clearing up measures were carried out in order to prevent any infections that could occur following the fact that these houses or apartments were abandoned. So, obviously, if there were any food items of animal origin, for example, because there was no electricity there, so we wanted to prevent any possible epidemics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What type of things would civilian defence remove from the houses once they entered?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: They removed foodstuff of plant or animal origin that were left behind. You know that nearly everybody at the time had large amounts of fresh meat in -- in the fridges or dry meat and other kinds of foodstuff, and due to the summer weather, this was a potential source of -- of epidemics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When civilian protection would enter these houses, would they be in uniform, on all occasions?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, they were wearing uniforms. If any member of the civilian protection did not have a full civilian protection uniform, this only occurred with people who carried out these duties for a long period of time, because the uniforms would -- would simply not be useable anymore, and we did not have replacement uniforms. The civilian protection also never entered any house or apartment without a police escort. This was a very clear instruction to all civilian protection units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How would the civilian protection enter a house if the house was locked?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: As I said, the civilian protection groups were escorted by the police and any such group also had an explosive expert who would carry out the initial examination of the door, first of all, before they entered, and then -- of the apartment. Obviously the circumstances in the month of August were such that possible stench or anything else that would provide the indication that there was a reason why the civilian protection had to intervene, in such cases, the civilian protection would force the door to enter the premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Zidovec, turning your attention to paragraph 34 of your statement. You say: "It is normal to expect larger amount of criminal activity in the area after such a large operation." Can you tell us why there would be an increase in criminality in that area?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: This statement that I made to the investigators is obviously partly a result of my general experience, because we have all witnessed a range of such turning-point activities, and this was just one of them. In addition, everything that happened in the first days after the completion of the combat activities in that area, brought about certain emotions which could not at all exclude the possibility of criminal activities. Once this area was opened, people went there for a variety of motives. There were refugees, displaced persons, but also criminals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the border with Bosnia was secure?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: One part of the border with Bosnia was covered by the police stations. However, this is a rather porous border, and that part which is usually called green border was such that one could cross it without any real risk or without any possibility of the police controlling the entire area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, could I seek clarification of the previous answer of the witness. You said: "Everything that happened in the first day after the completion of the combat activities brought about certain emotions which could not at all exclude the possibility of criminal activities." Now have I never heard of emotions which would exclude for the possibility of criminal activities. But could you tell the Chamber what you actually wanted to say here? Is it to say that emotions emerged which would drive people to acts of a criminal nature which, under other circumstances, they would not have committed? Is that what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I wanted to say that there was a very realistic possibility for the property that was in the area to be stolen, for various reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as I understood in paragraph 34, you were only talking about expectations. But leaving that apart, so what you wanted to say is that after Operation Storm, you could expect a higher level of theft. Now in the next line, you say that there were refugees, displaced persons but also criminals. Now, I do understand that criminals have an inclination to, at least if they are thieves, to theft, anyhow. So what then is the special emotion? Because this Chamber heard a lot of times that people were sometimes emotional because they saw that all their own property had been stolen or had been destroyed earlier and, although not being criminals, that they would take what they think was taken from them. These were not criminals. Now, what did you intend to say there, that it was only criminal that would commit theft or -- and what special emotions would have played a role there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as emotions are concerned, I'm referring to refugees and returnees in that respect. When I'm mentioning criminals, I'm quite clearly referring to certain individuals who engaged in crime for personal gain and had no other links to that area than crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me then see whether I understood your answer well. You had criminals who are stealing just because they wanted to become richer, and there were other people that, under the emotions of possibly revenge or possibly because they saw that their property had been taken by others and sought compensation, and that they may have been, for those reasons, inclined to take goods that may not have belonged to this them. Is that how I have to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think that the motive of revenge was quite understandable under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, could you also try to elicit from -- I sometimes need a rather long exegetical exercise in order to understand what the witness really wants to say. Could you please, also in the way in which you question him, try to get answers which are understandable for normal people as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going have to pass that task on to my colleague, Mr. President, because I have completed my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zidovec.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have got one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next, Cermak Defence. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: As things stand, Your Honour, no questions thank you. No questions, then for the Markac Defence. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Zidovec, you will now be examined by Mr. Mikulicic. And Mr. Mikulicic is counsel for Mr. Markac. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Zidovec.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will have several questions for you and since we speak the same language, we should be mindful of the fact that we need to make a pause between question and answer so that the interpreters can do their job. After I put a question to you, please wait with your answer so that the interpretation can catch up. Mr. Zidovec, mention was made of the uniforms of the civil protection, and you explained that, due to the objective circumstances, it was not always the case that the special -- that the civil protection units of wore uniforms. At any rate, can you tell what was the colour of the civilian protection uniform at the time, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: The civilian protection uniforms were of a greyish/greenish/brownish colour, although brown was the predominant colour. The uniforms had a sign of the civilian protection which clearly identified them. The insignia was envisaged the under the civilian protection convention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On the issue of the insignia, is it right that it was a blue triangle against an orange background?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] I would just like to draw your attention that that type of sign could be find under the Annex 1 to Additional Protocol of Geneva Convention from 12th of August, 1949, in paragraph 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zidovec, the civilian protection team which went out into the field on request consisted as you told us of a scene-of-crime officer, a civilian protection officer, and an explosives expert. Now the role of the scene-of-crime officer, in relation to the examination of a dead body and within the civilian protection team was exactly what?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: His main role was to preserve the location where the body was found and to preserve the trace evidence; in other words, the finger-prints, and to take a photograph of the body. Thus, preserving the state and condition of the body before sanitation takes place. Whenever it was possible, the body was searched for possible ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was the scene-of-crime officer precisely the person who was authorised to establish if, on the basis of the examination of the body, there were any indications of foul play?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: Yes. The scene-of-crime officer would examine the body and have the first indications of the possible cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I understand the procedure correctly, and you'll correct me if I'm wrong, there were two basic courses of action, the first being the following. If the scene of crime does not conclude that there was any foul play in relation to the body, what follows next is the removal of the body. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the event of the other situation, where the scene-of-crime officer, upon examining the body, suspects that murder may have been committed, another type of procedure will follow. Can you explain what that procedure was.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: According to this procedure and on the basis of the detailed crime report produced by the scene-of-crime officer, the crime police would, as part of the police administration, take further steps in the investigation, proceeding from the evidence collected during the scene of crime investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is my understanding correct, that in this case, the scene-of-crime officer would send his report also to the relevant crime police about the reasons to suspect that a crime had been committed?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: All the reports produced by scene of crime officers ended up in police administrations, including the ones you referred to, and the ones where it became obvious that the bodies concerned were to be found there as a result of combat activities and other type of activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was this a two-fold procedure. According to one, it was the police administrations that received information; and according to the other, it was the civilian protection that received information.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The hygiene and sanitation reports were produced and ultimately sent to the staff of OA Povratak, OA Return, and they were in fact produced by civilian protection bodies, were they not?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that the reports produced by scene of crime officers about possible crimes also ended up in the hands of the civilian protection bodies and the staff of the OA Povratak?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: These sort of reports did not reach the civilian protection structure. As you could see from the forms that were shown here, we only entered the data envisaged by the format of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The sanitation process you described for us during your testimony, you, as a high-ranking officer -- official of the Ministry of the Interior, did you ever receive instructions or orders, formally or informally, to the effect that the sanitisation process should be used as a method of suppressing evidence of crime as a method of covering up for foul play, crime, murder, arson, looting, and such-like?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us move to a different topic now. In your statement, and I'm referring to paragraph 39 - this is D1570 - you say that in late August and early -- or early September 1995, you visited Gracac. To the best of your recollection, what was the condition of the town when you got there? And I'm referring to the buildings, the streets, and so on?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: In the part of town where I moved, it was practically intact. I spent most of the time at the police station, i.e., in the same building housing the police station of the Krajina police. The building did not have any damage traces. It needed a good cleaning but nothing more than that. Close to that building there was a motel whose -- the name of which escapes me now, which was not damaged either. But that time, meals were provided there, both to the civilian protection units of and policemen. The civilian protection was billeted in a tent close to the police station. According to what I heard, a unit of the Special Police was to be found there at the time, and I knew General Markac and others among them, so I wanted to go and say hello. I took the civilian protection vehicle, and I went to the facility where they were, some 3 to 4 kilometres away from the police station. There, I found several individuals I knew. I spent perhaps half an hour talking to them on some vital matters, how they were faring, et cetera. I did not have to do the civilian protection business or that of the Special Police. It was a private conversation which lasted roughly half an hour. At that point members of the Special Police did say that they would appreciate it if the civilian protection unit cleaned the premises where they were quartered, and we merely engaged witty jokes about us not being able to afford, by that time, to pose as housekeeping help.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zidovec, now that you have broached the topic, the visit to the HQ of the Special Police in Gracac, how did it strike you in terms of the level of equipment and the conditions in which the Special Police were dwelling?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, they had a rather large room with tables put together and chairs, and I seem to recollect a computer being there. I know that an individual from the technical -- operational technical sector accompanied the Special Police contingent, and I presumed that the computer was his.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you perceived that room to be more of an office, an administrative office; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As you travelled through the area liberated in Operation Storm, you said you came across check-points; do you recall that? This is my question: Do you remember who it was who manned the check-points? What sort of units were they?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: The check-points were manned by the civilian police, sporting blue uniforms and by reserve [as interpreted] police forces, which had a different colour uniform; it was greyish/blue. The pattern was different and distinct from the regular police blue uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zidovec, you could recognise members of the reserve police by their uniforms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: Of course. Of course, members of Special Police wore uniforms of a distinct green colour, which differentiated them from all other police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... on page 63, line 10, was wrongly interpreted my question in respect of the type of police that I mentioned. I mentioned special, not reserve police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then that's now on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is what, therefore, the witness may have understood to be your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, the witness understood correctly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question to you, Mr. Zidovec. Did you ever see members of Special Police on the check-points? So were any of the check-points manned by Special Police members?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will first have a break before you have an opportunity to cross-examine the witness, Mr. Carrier. We will resume at a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zidovec, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Carrier. Mr. Carrier is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Carrier, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Zidovec, I have one introductory question. I just want to figure out, were you a member of the Command Staff of Operation Povratak?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: In the Command Staff of the Operation Povratak, there were all the competent assistant ministers, including myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: When you gave your statement to OTP and the Prosecution investigators back in 2007, at that time you told them that you didn't really remember much about Povratak. You said that you didn't directly participate in that operation. You said that it was primarily a police operation. You said you seemed uncertain to even -- who was in charge of that operation. Can you explain how it is as a member of the Command Staff of Operation Povratak you told the investigators that, and how come now you say that you were involved in that operation?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: This, first of all, had to do with a large of period of time which elapsed since these events. I was in charge of the civilian defence and fire-fighting exclusively in 1995 and never thereafter. And in 2001, I retired, and, at that point, I simply turned my attention towards some other activities, and I did not discuss these matters anymore. So the 12 years is certainly a long period of time which influenced what I said during that interview, and I also did not have any time to prepare for that interview. This is why my answer was to imprecise.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So I do understand you to say that, since 2007, you started to look at documents and then you realized or remembered that you actually were a member of Operation Povratak. Is that how it worked?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: This is not entirely true. After my interview with the investigators, possibly a year or so later, I was invited by the Defence team. And during that conversation we tried to extend some of my recollections. So between that moment of time and my arrival here, another year has elapsed. Once I was invited by the Defence to appear here, I started looking up certain documents or start -- tried to contact certain people who worked at the civilian protection at the time, in order to immerse myself into this subject. And before my arrival here, I also had an opportunity -- a couple of days of day before my arrival, I also had an opportunity to look at my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: You mentioned that in 1994 civil protection was moved from the Ministry of Defence, and then it came under the authority of the Ministry of the Interior, and was under your authority during 1995. I take it that when the authority was given to the MUP over civil protection, it was simply over the existing structure that was in place, that had existed since 1991.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: I do not understand precisely. Which structures are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: You said in your statement that civil protection had existed since 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, and it was an integral part of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And that's the structure that you took over -- or your ministry took over in 1995 and you were in charge of during 1995.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: No. The structure of civilian protection, fire-fighting, and fire prevention was set up in January of 1994 when civilian protection was moved from the Ministry of Defence to the Ministry of Interior. And there was another assistant minister who was in charge of that for a period of one year. When he left the ministry towards the end of 1994, in the early days of 1995, the minister made a decision whereby I was to be in charge of these segments, most probably he believed that in this way we could cover these issues without hiring a new assistant minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Okay. If a member of the military had asked that civilian protection personnel from the MUP be transferred to their groups for sanitations purposes, would you have been informed of that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: I suppose I would, either directly or by people belonging to the civilian protection which received such a request.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And during Operation Storm, Mr. Cemerin, who was the chief of civilian protection, he was on the ground during that operation and monitoring civilian protection; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: That's right. He supervised and coordinated the work of our units and our people on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And he would have been reporting to you about what his observations were, in terms of what was happening with civil protection sanitation operations after Operation Storm; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: Yes. Apart from general information that I received from him, I also received his opinions as to what needed to be improved, in order to carry out our tasks better. And also, within the civilian protection department, some of those tasks were -- some of these decisions were made by himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Zidovec, I didn't ask you about improvements or anything like that. I just wanted to know whether or not he did in fact he did report to you. So just to move it along a little more quickly, if you could just answer the question I pose to you. Now in your 2007 statement to the Prosecution, you said that civil protection had exclusive authority to collect bodies of people killed during Operation Storm. You said that you conducted that work completely independently from the military. In your supplemental statement you explain that perhaps you had some logistical support from the army, although you don't know the details of that. You also said that during your testimony today that perhaps there was some communication with the military, at least with respect to figuring out whether it was safe to conduct a sanitation operation. But you also say that civil protection never acted on orders from the HV Main Staff. And in your statement in 2007 you said that there was no formal or official communication with the military on collecting dead people. You also said that you were not aware of the military having conducted any sanitation operations during Operation Storm. Mr. Zidovec, I am going to suggest that, actually, none of that is accurate, and that in fact the MUP civil protection sanitation units that were under your authority including MUP civil protection personnel that you personally appointed to coordinator positions during Operation Povratak, not only coordinated their human sanitation activities with the HV but they also worked under the supervision of the HV to quickly sanitize the liberated territory of bodies after Operation Storm. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: I have no information about this. And I might add that during the conversations that I had these days, with people who used to work in the civil protection, including Mr. Cemerin and others, I was told categorically by them that military bodies did not participate in the sanitation operations carried out by civil protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: You mentioned today and in your supplemental statement from July 2009 that you maintain the position that you had exclusive authority for human sanitation, but you didn't discount the possibility that HV provided some logistical support, although you're not sure if they did do that in fact. I'm going to suggest to that there wasn't an order from the Split Military District logistics group before Operation Storm ordering support, in terms of manpower, supervision, among other things, for sanitation after the operation. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could I please have document number 65 ter 4503.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Zidovec, what's coming up on the screen in front of you is a Split Military District logistics order for Operation Storm dated the 1st of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: If we could go to page 6 in both English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And you'll see on this page it reads that: "Human sanitation shall be performed daily in cooperation with police administrations."

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And if we can go to page 10 in both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Zidovec, item number 11 of this logistics order is entitled "Sanitation of the Theatre of Operations." Item 11.1 indicates that the medical service of the HV command shall be responsible for the sanitation of the theatre of operations. Item 11.2 says basically that HV units of themselves can sanitize if it can be done quickly. Item 11.4 indicates that the HV will supply resources and troops to perform the sanitation with joint forces and that if the military isn't able to provide sufficient troops, the civilian institutions will be engaged, as required. Item 11.5 indicates that human sanitation will be carried out under the supervision of qualified HV personnel, and they list some, and one of them can be an army medical unit. And then just below item 11.5 in the next paragraphs, it's indicated that appropriate logistics base medical service in whose area of responsibility the sanitation is being formed will provide the necessary forensic experts. Now, Mr. Zidovec, given this logistics order from the Split Military District before Operation Storm, is it your position that you weren't aware that this order was made, that these resources were ordered to be supplied, that forensics experts were ordered to be supplied, all in support of human sanitation operations?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: No. Is this is the very first time that I have seen this document, and as regards to your final question, I have to answer negatively, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: During your examination today, Mr. Zidovec, you were shown an order from General Cervenko, which is Exhibit D598.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could please call that up onto the screen. I'm sorry, I've just been reminded that I'd like to tender the logistics order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think we need an updated translation of it, which I think is of some significance. So subject to the updated translation, 11.1 doesn't say Croatian armed forces; it says Croatian forces, which are two different terms, which will be relevant later. Subject to that, we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So no objection against the original, although would you like to have the translation verified. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit P2570.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. May I take it that you'll share your concerns about the translation with Mr. Carrier and that either he or you, together, will take care that we finally get the translation we need. That is, a fully accurate translation, especially if is on vital points of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Zidovec, were you aware that -- of General Cervenko's order back in August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I was not aware of it. Or I should perhaps say I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Registrar, could we have D598 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, could we have a clarification of that last answer. You were asked whether you were aware of this order. Now awareness can be the result of looking at the document, hearing about the document or whatever other information you would have received about an order. You then said: "Or I should perhaps say I didn't see it." The question was not, I think, whether you had seen the order. The question was whether you were aware of the existence of that order. Now, I do understand that you haven't seen it. Were you by any other means aware of such an order to exist, whether or not in writing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this moment my answer is negative. I wasn't aware of it. But what I do know is that in one or two orders received the previous day during the day, on the 4th of August, we sent almost identical instructions from the civilian protection to our units in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 and point number 2 on that page in both the English -- well, it may be page 1 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Point number 2, Mr. Zidovec, reads that: "In coordination with the police administrations and health Crisis Staff in the counties, include a civil protection unit from a county police administration ..." and it goes on to give different districts. And then the next paragraph, under number 2 it says that: "In the course of the work of the sanitation detachment, the commander of the detachment or a person designated by him, shall coordinate all issues concerning the implementation of the sanitization task within the scope of authorities of the counties."

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Now, you agree with me that it's -- that order indicates that part of the detachments formed for human sanitation by the HV are to include civil protection units as well.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: I don't know that civil protection units belonged to detachments that were set up by the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: General Cervenko's order indicates that if a detachment is set up, civil protection units are to form part of that; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: Yes, this is what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Point number 3 from this order from this order, which at the bottom of page 2 and on to page 3 of the English - still page 1 of the B/C/S - reads that: "Sanitation shall be conducted in accordance with the instructions of the Ministry of Defence." And it goes on to give details about that order, which is dated 15 October 1993, as well as the International Laws of War and then it lists some priorities. The first one being removal of corpses. Now, Mr. Zidovec, in your 2007 statement you indicated that you had you never heard of a military doctor named Dr. Brkic. We'll come back to that. This Chamber has already received evidence that Exhibit D1058 is an order from Dr. Brkic which outlines how human sanitation, among other things, is to be conducted. Were you ever aware of any order from an HV Main Staff doctor about how human sanitation was to be conducted?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Now point number 7 in General Cervenko's order appoints Brigadier Dr. Zlatar from the HV Main Staff to coordinate, supervise, and provide expert advice to the participants in the sanitation campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I get a clarification from counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Exhibit D1058 doesn't appear to be the document that Mr. Carrier claimed it would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: D1056, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And this person who is appointed to supervise, et cetera, is to coordinate and determine the procedure regarding corpses, carcasses, scattered livestock, et cetera. Now you agree that what is being described here is what you say came under your authority for civil protection. Is that not right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Zidovec, were you ever aware of an order issued by General Cermak during August 1995 regarding sanitation operations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Misetic, I have to note an objection. I finally pulled up D1056, and in the future if counsel could call up the documents so we have a chance to make our objections on time to the proposition that was posited, I don't believe accurately reflects what the document sates. So just so that we don't move too fast before we can make our objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that Mr. Carrier did not do it intentionally, but he is urged to be very precise so as to give a fair chance to the Defence to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, the document is dated 15 October 1993. So that date relevant in -- in light of what the witness testified happen in 1994, and I don't think it was accurately depicted as to what the contents of the document are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed at this moment, Mr. Carrier, I think you --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, in light of what you just said, if Mr. Carrier can provide to us the exhibit number for the document he is referring to at the moment, that would help me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Zidovec, are you aware that the military set up sanitation detachments at both the garrison and Military District level during Operation Storm and that civil protection personnel and units were incorporated into those structures?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: No. No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you please call up Exhibit P506, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zidovec, as we wait for this to come on to the screen, this is an order dated 5 August 1995, this time from General Cermak who is the HV Knin garrison commander. And this is an order issued to institute organised and expert hygenic and sanitation measures in relation to human an animal remains in the liberated area. You've never seen this order, though; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Now on page 1 you can see that General Cermak is ordering a terrain and hygiene sanitation measures staff under his command. And you can see he appoints a number of people. The first one being Brigadier Dr. Brkic, the Main Staff officer, as the head of staff. And just so we're clear this is the same doctor that wrote the Ministry of Defence instructions on hygiene and sanitation, dated 15 October 1993. That was a document mentioned in General Cervenko's order that we already looked at. You can see there are other people appointed as -- other army people appointed as head of human hygiene and sanitation measures. That is Major Sruk. There's a Lieutenant Dr. Snezija [phoen] - I know I'm pronouncing that probably very incorrectly - but that doctor was appointed as assistant head for human hygiene and sanitation measures. And you can see another person appointed was Captain Boris Radovic, and he was appointed coordinator for animal hygiene and sanitation measures. Were you ever aware of these people? You already said you don't know Dr. Brkic, but do you recognise the other names at all?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that this order by General Cermak seems to be setting up a team to deal with, among other things, organised and expert sanitation of human remains in the liberated area?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to my learned friend's question. The witness has already said he has never seen the document. Mr. Carrier is simply characterizing the document and asking the witness who has never seen the document before to confirm the contents of the documents, what the document represents itself to be. I don't see any point to that question at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, what the -- this order seems to be setting up, if you ask that from a witness who has never seen the document before, then you invite the witness to do something even the Chamber could do. That is, to see what the documents tell us. If you have any further questions in relation it that, of course, you may put them to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you please call up document number 65 ter 7342.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Zidovec, what is coming on to the screen here is a document that you issued on 7 August 1995 under the heading Operation Povratak. And it was sent to the Zadar-Knin police administration operative staff, and in that document you explain that your goal is to coordinate hygiene and sanitation measures in that police administration. And you particularly mention the town of Knin. Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And can you see that you have appointed a Mr. Cicko who was a senior advisor in the MUP civilian protection department. He was appointed to position of coordinator for hygiene and sanitation measures in Knin. Do you recall whether or not he actually accepted that appointment and went to Knin to work?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: He was in Knin, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And another person that you appoint is Dr. Sugnetic. I think I'm getting that quite wrong. And he was also a senior advisor with -- or, sorry, just an advisor with the Ministry of the Interior's civilian protection department, and you appointed him as deputy coordinator. Do you know whether or not that doctor took that up position and went on to the ground and helped coordinate human sanitation operations?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: I don't recall the name specifically or whether he was there, but I do know for a fact that Mr. Cicak was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Were you aware that in August 1995 General Cermak requested that Mr. Cicko and presumably the other doctor, although the name is misspelled, General Cermak requested that these people be transferred to the terrain hygiene and sanitation's measure staff under Dr. Brkic. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: If I could tender that document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that'll become Exhibit P2571.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd just like to make one point. And again, it's related to Mr. Carrier not announcing the exhibit numbers. If you actually look at the exhibit that he is referring to, and it's D1048, it doesn't quite say what Mr. Carrier is saying. And I know Your Honour, often makes the point about accuracy. It broadly says what Mr. Carrier is saying, but it certainly doesn't mention Dr. Brkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, if there is a specific or if there is a repeated comment on the accuracy of a summary or a quote of a document, then you will have to first show the original and then take us to the passage you want to summarise or you want to quote so that we can verify whether it's accurate. This has been raised now two times, so I invite you to show us, for the next two or three documents, that you always accurately summarise or quote. And give us an opportunity to verify.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Certainly. The next exhibit is D1058. The one after that is 65 ter 2096. The one after that is D603. And, Mr. Registrar, if could I have Exhibit D1058 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Zidovec, this is a request from General Cermak dated 10 August 1995 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- if you just wait for a second so that we have the document in both languages on our screen, as we have them now. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And can you see the subject heading is "Request for the transfer the personnel from the civil defence." And in this request, General Cermak states: "In regard to the sanitation of the municipality of Knin, we request the transfer of personnel from the MUP civil defence of the city of Zagreb to the staff for the sanitation of the terrain of the municipality of Knin with the aim of improving efficiency." And one of the people listed is the person that you had appointed, Damir Cicko. And I take it you're not in a position to confirm whether there was a Dr. Santetic, who was a member of civil defence, or is that a misspelling of -- do you know if that person exists as a member of civil defence?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: I can tell you nothing about the person under number 2. I simply can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And I take it you don't remember whether or not you received this request from General Cermak or whether you granted it or anything?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: No, I can't. In view of the addressee to which this -- or, rather, the address that was involved, he -- the letter would not have come to me for my information but to the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: But you would have been aware of the request, given that this is a request for transfer of civilian protection staff to -- to the HV.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't say anything specific about it, confirm it, or deny it, because I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next exhibit is going to be D30 and D612 after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Zidovec, do you recall whether or not you ever received any reports or any subsequent interactions on the ground during the sanitation process between Mr. Cicko and Dr. Brkic.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Do you know a person who was employed as an engineer during August 1995 named Ivan Jelic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: I don't even know where the person was employed. The name doesn't tell me anything. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have Exhibit D30 up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Zidovec, this is a report from Dr. Brkic to General Cermak dated 12 August 1995, and he's reporting on hygiene and sanitation measures taken in the period from 5 to 12 August 1995. And in this report, he indicates that he arrived in Knin on the 5th of August, 1995. And on page 1 and on to page 2 in the English, but still in page 1 in the B/C/S, under heading 1, which is human sanitation and technical measures, Dr. Brkic talks about arriving in the Knin city cemetery, discovering that there was an excavator, there's was a hole, there were several bodies around the hole and in the hole. Also indicates that exact numbers of bodies would have been indicated in the daily report. And he talks about an interaction with Ivan Jelic. And if you go down to the next paragraph, he talks about arriving back in the cemetery on 7 August 1995 to discover that the hole had been filled in, and he made inquiries as to who had filled it in; he didn't get an answer. He talked about how he realized his presence there was indispensable due to the work and actions that they were performing. And he goes on to say that together with the civilian protection staff, pursuant to General Cermak's order, they produced certain results which conformed with all the rules of hygiene and sanitation measures and talks about having to deal with the bodies in a different way. And then down at the next paragraph, Dr. Brkic indicates that this work certainly could not have been carried out without civil protection and specifically names Mr. Cicko, among others. Were you ever aware or made aware from Mr. Cicko, the person you appointed or anyone else about any involvement with an army doctor?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC
utterances.text: In our dealings, there were no army doctors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, I would need a couple of minutes for a few procedural matters. We have only a couple of minutes left. Therefore, my question whether this would be a suitable moment needs only one answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zidovec, we'll adjourn for the day. We'd like to you back tomorrow in the afternoon at a quarter past 2.00 in this same courtroom. Meanwhile, I instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether it is the testimony you gave already today or whether it's testimony still to be given tomorrow. I'll ask Madam Usher to escort you out of the courtroom, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to read quickly the reasons for a decision which was taken already quite a while ago. These are the Chamber's reasons for granting trial-related protective measures for Witness AG-58. In court on the 9th of June, 2009, during closed session, the Gotovina Defence applied for full protective measures for Witness AG-58. This request can be found at transcript page 18.405. Neither the Prosecution nor the Cermak or Markac Defence objected. On the same day, the Chamber granted the application and decided that it would hear the testimony of Witness AG-58 in closed session and refer to the witness by his pseudonym. This decision can be found at transcript page 18.410, and the decision was rendered in closed session and the public is hereby informed about it. This Chamber has previously held that a party seeking protective measures for a witness must demonstrate an objectively grounded risk to the security or welfare of the witness or the witness's family, should it become known that the witness has given evidence before this Tribunal. The mere expression of fear by a witness is insufficient to justify protective measures. This standard can, for example, be satisfied by showing that a threat was made against the witness or the witness's family. Witness AG-58, a Croatian Serb, lives with his family in Serbia. The witness feared that, should it become known that he had testified, the security and welfare of his family in Serbia might be put at risk. The witness's fear was based on two incidents that occurred just before he left for The Hague. On one occasion, he repeatedly noticed that a certain person or persons in his vicinity appeared to be following him. On another occasion, he encountered an acquaintance, who made comments that were delivered in a way and contained allusions such that the witness could, and did, reasonably perceive them as a warning about his family's security or welfare. The Gotovina Defence stated that these comments were made after the witness informed his acquaintance that he was called to testify by the Gotovina Defence. None of the other parties explored this assertion, which was made at transcript page 18.352. For these reasons, the Chamber found that the Gotovina Defence had demonstrated an objectively grounded risk to the security and welfare of Witness AG-58 and his family, should it become known that he had given evidence before this Tribunal. The Chamber furthermore considered that, in light of the nature of the anticipated evidence of the witness, the only effective way to protect his identity was to hear his testimony in closed session. And this concludes the Chamber's reasons for its decision to grant protective measures to Witness AG-58. Next matter. Very briefly, the Chamber was informed that Mr. Markac would prefer not to be present in court on the 13th of July. This is understood as a waiver of the right to be present during that day, and if it's for personal reasons that Mr. Markac prefers not to be present, then the Chamber doesn't need any further information. If, however, there would be other reasons which would be of a kind for the Chamber to know, the Chamber would expect Mr. Kuzmanovic or Mr. Mikulicic to inform the Chamber in an appropriate way. Then, finally, we turn into private session for one second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Finally, Mr. Carrier, could you give us an indication as to how much time you would still need for your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I hope to complete it in the first session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first session. Then anything unusual long for re-examination or just within the normal limits which is anything between five and ten minutes? Then we adjourn, and we resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 8th of July, quarter past 2.00, Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 8th day of July, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.
